newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Report brands Belgian child sex probe incompetent.
newsitem.headline: Report brands Belgian child sex probe incompetent.

text.p: Police investigating Belgium's scandal of kidnapped, abused and murdered children were branded as arrogant and autocratic in leaked extracts from a special report on Monday.
Magistrates were insensitive and slow to act, according to the report, which will be handed to party leaders on Tuesday and debated on Thursday and Friday.
It follows six months of often televised hearings by a parliamentary commission that alternately gripped and revolted the nation.
As the extracts were published in La Derniere Heure newspaper on Monday, police began digging again for evidence at an abandoned mining complex in a suburb of the central city of Charleroi
They dug there in December and January, finding nothing. But echo-sounding equipment has found an unexplored gallery.
A convicted child rapist, Marc Dutroux, is facing murder charges arising from the investigation.

"It is striking to find that in Charleroi there was not only no follow-up to the investigations...but no attention was paid to the follow-up and analysis of the inquiries into Dutroux," the newspaper cited the report as saying.
The scandal came to light in mid-August when Dutroux was arrested after an alert eyewitness identified his van near where 14-year-old Laetitia Delhez had gone missing a few days earlier.

Dutroux led police to a hidden cell in the basement of a house he owned in Charleroi where they found Laetitia and 12-year-old Sabine Dardenne, who had gone missing three months earlier. Both girls were alive but had been sexually abused.
Father-of-three Dutroux then led police to the buried bodies of eight-year-olds Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo who had died of starvation the previous March, nine months after being abducted.
Less than three weeks later, Dutroux led police to the buried bodies of teenagers An Marchal and Eefje Lambrecks.
Last month the body of eight-year-old Belgian-born Moroccan girl Loubna Benaissa was found stuffed into a steel trunk in the basement of a Brussels garage near her home.
Convicted child abuser Patrick Derochette, who according to newspapers has admitted keeping her alive for at least a day, has been charged with illegal imprisonment and rape leading to her death.

As investigations got under way it emerged that gendarmes had been watching Dutroux for years but had failed to curtail his activities or inform magistrates investigating the disappearances that he was a key suspect with a history.

In October more than 250,000 people marched through Brussels in sympathy with the victims and their parents, but also as a show of disgust at a system seen by most as incompetent and by some as somehow having protected Dutroux.
Between October and March the parliamentary commission interviewed 110 people, from magistrates to police and parents.
Last week other leaked extracts of the report listed a catalogue of errors.

It said investigators were slow to get onto the cases, ignored vital evidence, were cold and dismissive towards parents, jealously guarded key information, had insufficient resources and used them badly and in a completely uncoordinated manner.
The government has promised reforms, and at the weekend a team of investigators flew to the United States to start special training with the Federal Bureau of Investigation.
Unless the reforms bear fruit, and unless heads roll, there is likely to be a bigger and angrier repeat of the October march.
The commission's report will not be the last word. It has been given until September 30 to follow up its theory that Dutroux may have had high level protection.
